title: 3-Read Friday #67: Adaptive Teaching, Curse of Knowledge, and Cognitive Ventriloquism
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #67 of 3-Read Friday leads with Matthew Evans's attempt to give 'adaptive teaching' a tight, defensible definition -- teachers adapting to in-the-moment feedback during a lesson -- distinguishing it sharply from differentiation and broader inclusive teaching, which Barton flags as a genuinely useful conceptual clarification. Blake Harvard follows with a Rubik's Cube demonstration of the curse of knowledge, arguing teachers routinely underestimate how cognitively demanding it is to process brand-new material once, a point Barton calls an important reminder. Carl Hendrick closes with the Clever Hans story as a lens on 'cognitive ventriloquism' -- the ways teachers unconsciously cue students toward correct answers, producing an illusion of understanding that masks the absence of real learning. Barton frames all three as variations on a single theme: the gap between what looks like understanding in the moment and what a student can actually do independently.
points: Evans's tight definition of adaptive teaching -- responding to moment-to-moment feedback during the lesson, not before-lesson planning or general inclusive practice -- is designed specifically to prevent 'concept creep' that dilutes the term into meaninglessness.

Harvard's Rubik's Cube demonstration makes the curse of knowledge experiential rather than abstract: readers who just watched a 5-minute tutorial and still can't solve the cube directly feel what students experience after a single explanation of new material.

Hendrick's four mechanisms of cognitive ventriloquism (unconscious cueing, question framing, environmental scaffolding, feedback patterns) give teachers a specific taxonomy for auditing their own unconscious cueing behavior, not just a general warning.

Barton's synthesis: all three pieces converge on the same underlying trap -- performance in the moment (a right hinge answer, a solved practice problem, a class that seems to follow along) is a poor and sometimes misleading proxy for durable, independent understanding.
quotes: Matthew makes a compelling case that adaptive teaching is not just differentiation in disguise.
Our starting point should be to design high-quality, inclusive instruction, regularly get data on our students' understanding, and only then adapt.
An important reminder - along with a lovely example - of why one of the most important things a teacher needs to be aware of is the curse of knowledge.
Cognitve Ventriloquism is my new favourite phrase. Carl outlines what it is, why it is a problem, and the four mechanisms through which it may manifest.
